heading: BRANDED SEARCH IS BECOMING A LESS RELIABLE PROXY FOR BRAND DEMAND (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Branded search volume declined 11.1% over one month while the auction environment remained stable, challenging the long-held assumption that branded search reliably indicates brand demand. The article attributes this divergence to AI Overviews, which appeared in 95.9% of commercial searches by June 2026 (up from 57.2% less than 12 months prior), effectively answering consumer questions before they perform additional searches and shifting the decision-making process upstream. The author argues this is fundamentally a measurement problem rather than a demand problem: consumer preference may remain unchanged while observable search behavior has shifted due to AI intermediation. The consequence is that marketers relying on branded search as their primary demand proxy risk misallocating capital, potentially underinvesting in long-term brand building activities when they interpret declining branded search as weakening demand. The article recommends treating branded search as one indicator among several—including unaided awareness and share of search—and shifting investment toward activities that build authority and credibility with AI systems themselves.
strategic_hook: Understanding how changes in consumer research behavior and information-gathering channels (driven by AI) are reshaping what metrics actually reflect customer demand is essential for validating business strategy and reallocating resources away from increasingly misleading performance indicators.

heading: DOES TOPICAL AUTHORITY MATTER IN AI SEARCH? (7 MINUTE READ)
summary: A comprehensive study of 1,094 US categories covering over 220,000 domains found that topical authority remains important in AI search, though the landscape differs markedly from traditional Google Search. Only 15.2% of categories had a clear owner as of June 2026, with 89.3% of AI-search demand concentrated in categories lacking a dominant brand—creating a significant window of opportunity for challengers. Category owners retained their position 90.4% of the time month-over-month, but those with narrow leads (median 1.3-point advantage) were vulnerable to displacement by close runners-up, whereas leaders with wider margins (2.9+ points) proved durable. The study tracked 5,470 category comparisons and found that most cited domains were rarely the most-mentioned brands—a critical distinction because user behavior research shows users focus on brand mentions rather than citations when making purchase decisions. The data suggests that focused topical strategies targeting commercially important categories without clear owners, paired with gap-closing content across underrepresented prompts, offer the best return on content investment in AI search environments.
strategic_hook: Companies should prioritize customer-research activities to identify which commercially important product categories currently lack dominant owners in AI search systems, then map customer decision prompts (comparison, alternatives, buying intent) to identify content gaps where competitor mentions appear but yours do not.

heading: WHAT EVERYONE GETS WRONG ABOUT CATEGORY CREATION (6 MINUTE READ)
summary: Most companies misunderstand category creation by treating it as a naming exercise rather than identifying a genuine job-to-be-done (JTBD). Real category creation requires that a corresponding JTBD exists—a concrete responsibility that appears on someone's job description—and that a company's product solves that job end-to-end. Gong's annual rebranding from "Reality Platform" to "Revenue AI Platform" exemplifies this mistake; the category name changes yearly because no actual JTBD was created, whereas Salesforce's consistent "CRM" positioning since 2004 reflects a real underlying job. Clari's "Enterprise Revenue Orchestration" platform faces similar risks because "orchestrate revenue" is too broad and vague to represent a genuine JTBD; it encompasses hundreds of unmet sub-tasks that Clari's six products don't address. Rather than inventing abstract categories, companies should either create the missing JTBD first (as Clay did with "GTM engineering"), dissolve the platform into a suite of independent products, or lead with their strongest single product and upsell from there.
strategic_hook: Understanding whether a proposed category expansion maps to genuine customer jobs-to-be-done is essential for building a credible business case and avoiding failed positioning that wastes GTM resources on messaging that prospects cannot act upon.

heading: THOUGHTLESS FEATURES NEVER ADD UP TO A THOUGHTFUL PRODUCT (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article argues that products accumulate thoughtless features because stakeholders propose solutions without understanding actual user needs, and these ideas ship before designers can intervene. The "ham biscuit sign" serves as an analogy for poorly conceived features that solve surface-level problems but create new ones—like an electrified sign warning of an electrified fence that doesn't actually communicate the danger. AI exacerbates this pattern by making it trivial to regurgitate common features from other products (dark mode, FAQ pages, task counters) without questioning whether they're necessary. The root cause is that teams ask "wouldn't it be cool if?" rather than studying actual user workflows, validating necessity, or understanding business value. Solutions include using Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks, the top tasks method, and focusing on failure cases instead of feature checklists, all of which require actual thinking about workflows rather than rapid feature generation.
strategic_hook: Understanding customer workflows and failure cases through structured research methods like JTBD and top tasks surveys is essential to validating which features genuinely serve customer needs versus adding noise to the product.

The platform is operated by Worldata, a direct response media agency with over 40 years of industry experience, and serves as a lead-generation funnel for Constant Contact's broader email marketing platform, which it offers to SubjectLine users at a 30% discount.

heading: RCS OR SMS? IT DEPENDS ON THE TASK (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Rich Communication Services (RCS), now available on 96% of U.S. mobile devices, offers ecommerce retailers a richer messaging alternative to SMS, comparable to how HTML transformed email capabilities. Unlike SMS's 160-character limit, RCS supports images, video, interactive buttons, and carousels, but typically costs at least twice as much and relies on data networks rather than cellular networks. The article applies the jobs-to-be-done framework to argue that RCS should only be adopted when its rich media features genuinely help customers complete specific tasks—such as evaluating products, recovering abandoned carts, confirming information, or choosing options—rather than merely as a technological upgrade. SMS remains preferable for simpler, urgent jobs like sending order confirmations, one-time passcodes, or delivery reminders that don't require visual or interactive elements. The article recommends testing both channels against similar customer segments and measuring success through task completion rates, conversion rates, and cost per completed action rather than engagement metrics like button clicks.
strategic_hook: Marketers should use the jobs-to-be-done framework to identify which customer communication tasks genuinely require RCS's richer capabilities versus which are better served by simpler SMS, then test both channels to build a business case for the higher RCS costs based on incremental conversion and profitability gains.

heading: AI IS WORKING OVERTIME. SO AM I (10 MINUTE READ)
summary: This article examines AI fatigue—the psychological and operational strain workers experience from widespread AI adoption—which now affects 16% of AI users according to a May 2026 Software Finder survey. Half of U.S. employees use AI on the job, yet 77% report it has increased their workload, with 39% spending more time reviewing AI-generated content and 23% spending more time learning tools. The core problem is that while AI accelerates generation time, it often extends overall completion time through verification, decision-making overhead, and "workslop" (polished but incorrect outputs that require full reworking). A 2026 meta-analysis of 22 studies concluded that AI fatigue stems not only from individual behavior but from poorly designed systems and unclear workplace policies around tool approval, data privacy, and usage guidelines. The article identifies four sources of strain: tool overload, verification burden, prompt exhaustion, and keeping-up anxiety, and provides tactical guidance—such as limiting prompts to three rounds, checking facts against two sources, setting AI-free focus blocks, and asking whether a task is truly lighter with AI or just creates more decisions to manage.
strategic_hook: none.

heading: THE BIGGEST TECHNICAL SEO TIME-WASTERS TO AVOID (6 MINUTE READ)
summary: The article argues that technical SEO professionals should stop pursuing activities based solely on audit tool warnings or best-practice checklists and instead focus on work with measurable business impact. It identifies common time-wasting tasks including chasing incremental Core Web Vitals improvements when scores are already "good," removing isolated redirects without chains, optimizing crawl budget on smaller sites where it isn't a constraint, fixing individual 404 errors that don't harm users, removing obsolete meta keywords, routinely updating disavow files, and clearing every tool alert. Instead, the author recommends prioritizing technical SEO work that directly impacts revenue or business goals, creates a foundation enabling other value-creating initiatives, or prepares the website for AI-driven search. The core principle is treating technical SEO as a business investment requiring clear ROI rather than box-checking exercise.
strategic_hook: When deciding which technical SEO initiatives to pursue, teams should map each initiative against specific business outcomes and customer impact—such as conversion rate improvement or user experience—rather than treating tool alerts as equally urgent priorities.

She shares that after investing in her online presence—particularly LinkedIn and Substack where she writes about content marketing—she now receives six LinkedIn recruiter messages annually and job opportunities come to her unsolicited rather than her chasing positions. Key tactics she recommends include: optimizing LinkedIn profiles with keywords for desired roles (not past roles), maintaining visibility on a single platform consistently, being generous with ideas and expertise, doing reliable work that makes people want to hire you again, and continuously learning to stay competitive. The author emphasizes that as hiring managers increasingly turn to referrals and headhunters to find passive candidates already employed, personal reputation has become far more valuable than a tailored CV.

summary: Lob, a direct mail platform, released an ebook titled "Thumb-stopping Mail" that outlines 30+ creative techniques for making direct mail campaigns stand out in crowded mailboxes, where recipients typically spend only three seconds deciding whether to engage. The ebook identifies seven essential elements for effective direct mail: visuals with high contrast and eye-catching imagery, bold headlines that signal relevance within seconds, scannable copy with clear hierarchy, strong calls-to-action with multiple response paths (QR codes, URLs, phone numbers), personalized value anchors, reduced cognitive friction through curation and specificity, and strategic urgency tied directly to offers rather than arbitrary deadlines. Drawing on analysis of over one billion mail sends, Lob emphasizes that the strongest pieces communicate with intention—avoiding information overload—and balance emotional appeal with logical, quantifiable benefits to drive recipient action. The ebook includes real-world examples demonstrating how real estate letters using neighborhood-specific mortgage comparisons, seasonal gift guides with organized recommendations, and savings account offers with transparent APY rates outperform generic communications by establishing trust and making the next step obvious.
strategic_hook: Understanding how customers process direct mail information and what specific design elements trigger engagement can directly inform customer journey mapping and message strategy for campaigns targeting prospects at different decision stages.

heading: AI CONTENT IS EVERYWHERE ON SOCIAL MEDIA, ESPECIALLY LINKEDIN (4 MINUTE READ)

Two-thirds of all flagged AI content came from LinkedIn despite representing only a third of scanned items, while X/Twitter had nearly 50% of articles that were either fully or partially AI-generated. Reddit had the lowest AI rate at 4.4% overall, but top-level posts showed an 11.6% AI rate, suggesting that AI content targets high-visibility formats across platforms. heading: OPENAI APPEARS TO BE MISSING ITS SALES GOALS BY A VAST MARGIN (2 MINUTE READ)
summary: OpenAI's advertising revenue is tracking toward massive shortfalls against its own projections. Emarketer estimates the entire addressable market for chatbot advertising at just $5.4 billion, and projects that OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon combined will generate under $1 billion in 2026—far below OpenAI's projection of $2.5 billion from ads alone by year-end. To hit its targets, OpenAI would need advertisers to abandon decades of investment in search and social platforms, simultaneously dominate against advertising giants like Google and Meta, and grow the AI ad market from six figures to a 12-figure business. Since advertising is supposed to represent 36 percent of OpenAI's total revenue by 2030 according to the company's own forecasts, missing these projections would undermine a major financial justification for the AI industry's massive capital expenditure.

heading: COPYWRITING BREAKDOWN: HOW TO SELL SOMETHING ORDINARY (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: Claude Hopkins's 1920s approach to selling Palmolive Shaving Cream demonstrates a three-step methodology that remains relevant today: first, conduct voice-of-customer research to discover what the market actually wants; second, measure your product against those specific desires with hard data rather than vague claims; third, be the first to publicly communicate those measured results. Hopkins interviewed hundreds of men and learned they wanted abundant lather, quick action on tough beards, and long-lasting lather. He then had Palmolive's chemist measure these qualities, producing specific figures: the cream multiplied itself 250 times in lather, the beard absorbed 15 percent water within one minute, and it retained creamy fullness for ten minutes. The resulting advertisement emphasized these research-backed specifications rather than relying on superlatives, making it persuasive enough to win customers from established competitors. Hopkins's insight was that most products in a category are functionally similar, but the company willing to invest in research and then own the first-mover advantage of stating common properties with data will outperform rivals.
strategic_hook: Understanding what customers actually want through structured research—rather than assumptions—should inform both messaging strategy and product positioning decisions, directly connecting customer needs research to conversion-focused copywriting and competitive differentiation.

heading: SWAG THAT WORKS: THE NEW RULES FOR TRADE SHOW GIVEAWAYS (5 MINUTE READ)

Research shows 82 percent of recipients feel more positive about a brand after receiving promotional products, and 87 percent keep and use them regularly. Success requires intentional strategy around product selection, multi-level engagement funnels, and integrated follow-up measurement; Middesk's approach generated 10 times the activation spend in new pipeline and 26 times in influenced pipeline, plus unexpected LinkedIn follower growth. The shift reflects broader recognition that quality, relevant merchandise creates community, reinforces brand narrative, and provides lasting touchpoints for sales and marketing teams to leverage post-event.
strategic_hook: Brands should map customer journey tiers within trade shows to inform merchandise strategy, ensuring gifting reinforces relationship value and enables sales teams to qualify and follow up with prospects based on engagement level.

heading: HOW THE FOUNDER OF MORNING BREW BUILT A CLAUDE CONTENT MACHINE THAT NEVER RUNS OUT OF IDEAS (43 MINUTE VIDEO)
summary: Alex Lieberman, co-founder of Tenex, has built an AI content system using Claude that automates idea discovery, drafting, and quality control while maintaining his distinct voice. The system scans his Slack, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notes daily to surface 15 ranked content ideas, then uses six interviewer personas (Tim Ferriss, Joe Rogan, Larry King, Howard Stern, Barbara Walters, Michael Barrow) to extract specifics through follow-up questions that he answers via voice-to-text. A personal voice guide encoded in Markdown—capturing his top-performing posts, hook formulas, and language patterns like "self-deprecating confidence"—ensures drafts are calibrated to how he actually writes rather than internet averages. The system routes completed drafts through a "Writer's Council" of six personas that score submissions and iterate until reaching a 9-out-of-10 threshold, while a reinforcement loop extracts lessons after publication to prevent repeated mistakes. Beyond the tool itself, Lieberman argues that employees are an underleveraged marketing channel and launched a "Creator Cup" with $5,000 in prizes to incentivize team content creation, which at his previous company Storyarb drove 40% of inbound leads in one quarter.

heading: HOW MUCH CREATIVE DEBT ARE YOU CARRYING? (6 MINUTE READ)
summary: Kevan Lee and Shannon Deep introduce the concept of "creative debt"—borrowing from future creative ambitions to handle present urgencies—which they argue accrues interest faster than any other type of debt. Using personal examples, including Lee's experience losing a weekly podcast outlet that had unknowingly offset his creative debt, the authors explain how postponed creative work compounds into identity-eroding narratives and regret. They outline nine strategies for addressing creative debt, from stopping new loans and making small "interest-only payments" to consolidating projects, creating automatic payment systems, and abandoning projects that no longer serve one's current self. The authors anchor their advice in their own practice of designating Fridays as protected creative time and promote their upcoming creative retreat called "The Excuse," scheduled for 2027 in the French countryside, as a vehicle for making lump-sum payments against accumulated creative debt.

heading: WHY YOUR TOP KEYWORDS ARE QUIETLY LOSING VOLUME (11 MINUTE READ)
summary: Brainlabs analysed 1.35 million UK search keywords across nine categories and found that head terms (1–3 words) are declining in volume in seven of nine categories, with entertainment down 16% year-on-year and travel down 5.2%, while longtail queries (4+ words) are growing significantly. AI Overviews appear on longtail queries at rates 2–3 times higher than head terms across all categories, with exposure ranging from 23.4% to 58.5% depending on category, and Google is deploying them conservatively on commercially sensitive head terms while aggressively on longtail. The research reveals that while Semrush's August 2025 study showed people still use Google at similar frequencies, query composition has fundamentally shifted toward longer, more specific searches, and users are increasingly finding answers in AI Overviews rather than traditional ranked results. For brands, this means ranking position one no longer guarantees traffic on longtail queries where AIOs sit above organic results, and success now requires three parallel objectives: traditional ranking, AIO citation visibility, and zero-click brand presence through source attribution.
strategic_hook: Understanding the structural shift from head to longtail query volume and AIO exposure rates directly informs how to segment target customers by search intent and develop differentiated content strategies that address whether customers are searching informational head terms that may soon migrate to AI tools or high-intent longtail queries where AIO citation has become a visibility objective equal to ranking.

heading: 10 CREATIVE WAYS TO WRITE WITH AI WITHOUT LOSING YOUR SOUL (15 MINUTE READ)

The approaches include "vibewriting" (iterative feedback-based drafting), the "Living Draft" method (continuously feeding ideas into an evolving piece), AI-conducted interviews, leveraging existing knowledge bases, data-driven article generation, brainstorming 100 angles then clustering them, and applying mental models to structure arguments. The article emphasizes that these techniques make previously difficult or expensive content creation feasible while maintaining authorial voice and strategic intent. Ahrefs demonstrates each method with real examples from their own content operations, including custom tools built on platforms like Letaido for automating data refreshes and synthesizing internal documentation.
strategic_hook: Understanding how to apply different AI-assisted workflows to content strategy helps marketers identify which discovery and research methods best serve their specific customer needs and content gaps, rather than defaulting to low-effort, generalized automation.

heading: HOW MICHELOB ULTRA AND LEO MESSI PREPARED FOR THE MOST UNPREDICTABLE MARKETING MOMENT OF THE WORLD CUP (3 MINUTE READ)

Michelob Ultra, Messi's partner since 2020 and the tournament's official beer sponsor, deployed the spot across social, digital channels, Telemundo's post-game show, and Times Square billboards. By structuring the creative around Messi's career rather than the final match outcome, the brand built flexibility into a campaign that worked regardless of whether Argentina advanced or was eliminated, solving the challenge of planning for real-time relevance around an uncontrollable event.

heading: THE B2B BLOG IS COLLAPSING. THE COMPANIES REPLACING IT ARE BECOMING PUBLISHERS (5 MINUTE READ)
summary: Traditional B2B blogs built on search optimization are collapsing as Google's AI Overviews reduce clickthrough rates—Google search traffic to publishers fell 33% globally by November 2025, and HubSpot lost 70-80% of organic traffic. Similarly, LinkedIn organic reach for company pages dropped 60-66% between 2024 and early 2026, from 7% reach to 1.6% of followers. Companies are replacing the blog playbook with "owned media" strategy: building actual publications with original reporting, interviews, and industry commentary that serve their ideal customer profile directly rather than algorithms. The owned media model creates compounding returns through person-to-person distribution, editorial conversations that double as pipeline, and content that gets syndicated and surfaced by AI systems without ongoing ad spend. The State of Brand, built by Outlever using this playbook, reached 1.5 million monthly unique visitors in three months with majority traffic from unpaid sources. Success is measured not by raw audience size but by what percentage of the target market actually reads, returns to, and trusts the publication as their industry source of record.
strategic_hook: Owned media strategy requires deep understanding of your actual ICP, what stories and voices matter to them, and where your brand genuinely fits in the industry narrative—directly informing customer research and market analysis work.

heading: FRENCH LAWMAKERS APPROVE A SWEEPING SOCIAL MEDIA BAN FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15 (3 MINUTE READ)

Legal experts noted significant implementation challenges around age verification and account suspension for existing underage users. The move follows Australia's 2024 ban on children under 16 and precedes similar restrictions being considered in Spain, Denmark, Greece, and the United Kingdom.

heading: WHEN AND HOW TO CALL CUSTOMERS BY NAME (3 MINUTE READ)
summary: Research from Monash University found that when service employees address customers by name, average spending increases 17.3 percent (from $28.67 to $33.64), upsell acceptance more than doubles from 22.6 percent to 48.4 percent, and customer satisfaction rises 15.9 percent. The recommendation is to train employees to use names naturally and sparingly, after introducing themselves first, avoiding contexts where privacy is preferred.

heading: HOW TO KNOW YOU'RE READY FOR A FRACTIONAL CMO AND HOW TO BRIEF ONE WELL (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: This article outlines the conditions under which a business should hire a fractional CMO and how to structure such an engagement effectively. A company is ready for a fractional CMO when it has a clear strategic gap—such as marketing decisions made by committee, strong product traction without a compelling narrative, or an approaching inflection point—combined with an existing execution layer (internal team, agency, or tools) but no one directing strategy. Conversely, businesses lack product-market fit, have no execution capability, or are seeking hands-on daily marketing work should not pursue fractional leadership. The article emphasizes that successful engagements depend on clear briefs that present business problems rather than task lists, shared financial data, honest failure history, defined decision rights, explicit cadence agreements, and time-bound 90-day markers rather than vague mandates. The author positions fractional CMO hiring as a fit-based decision, not a size-based one, where the cost-benefit works when a $250,000+ full-time hire isn't yet justified but strategic gaps are actively costing the business.
strategic_hook: A business evaluating whether to hire a fractional CMO should map its current marketing decision-making structure and execution capabilities against the five readiness signals to determine whether the strategic gap is real and addressable before engaging.

heading: MEASUREMENT IS A BUSINESS ADVANTAGE (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: Most marketing teams rely on default analytics tools and ad platform reporting, which creates blind spots that competitors can exploit. The article identifies four competitive advantages for teams that build rigorous measurement systems: accessing cheaper channels like podcasts and sponsorships that competitors dismiss as unmeasurable, sending better conversion signals to ad platforms to improve algorithmic targeting, discovering budget efficiencies through granular reporting (like VEED's finding that certain keywords attracted higher-ARPU subscribers), and avoiding "measurement debt"—the inability to evaluate marketing spend when clean baseline data was never collected. Standard click-based attribution struggles with multi-device journeys and non-click channels, pushing budget toward easy-to-track but increasingly expensive channels like paid search. The author argues that rough, honest measurement using multiple methods (surveys, signal metrics, attribution models) beats perfect measurement delayed indefinitely, and demonstrates the mechanism through VEED's restructuring around use cases, which grew subscriptions 20% while maintaining flat CAC.
strategic_hook: Understanding the varying lifetime value and retention characteristics of customers acquired through different channels and keywords is essential for building a customer-centric business case that properly allocates marketing spend.

heading: THE MOST VALUABLE THING APPLE BUILT IN THE 2000S WASN'T THE IPOD (4 MINUTE READ)
summary: Apple launched the iTunes Music Store on April 28, 2003, with approximately 200,000 songs priced at 99 cents each, surpassing its first-million-song sales forecast in just six days and reaching 70 percent of all legal digital music downloads within three years. The strategy worked by unbundling the album—the industry's traditional unit of value—into individual tracks, fundamentally shifting how music was packaged and priced. Jobs spent eighteen months personally negotiating with the five major label CEOs, deliberately positioning iTunes as a small Mac-only experiment rather than an industry-wide play, and accepted the labels' own proposal of 99-cent pricing. Beneath the surface, iTunes' real value was building the largest credit-card-on-file database in consumer tech, training millions of users to make frequent small purchases with a single tap—a frictionless payment foundation that would later power the App Store and unlock Apple's entire Services ecosystem, now worth over 100 billion dollars. The low iTunes margins were intentional; the iPod hardware was the actual product being marketed, with each song purchase serving as a low-friction habit builder for card-on-file spending.
strategic_hook: Understanding how to identify and unbundle the implicit product (music bundles) versus the explicit product (songs) reveals hidden customer needs and can unlock adjacent business opportunities beyond the immediate transaction.
